en: The Blessed Lord said:
Fearlessness, purity of heart, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, [and so forth].
Generosity, self-control, sacrifice, study of the sacred texts, austerity, and uprightness. //1//
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of malice, compassion toward all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness. (2)
Splendor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from malice, and lack of excessive pride—these belong to one born with divine fortune, O Bhārata. (3)
Śrīdhara:
Having abandoned the demoniac nature and taken refuge in the divine alone, men are liberated; to determine this, the discrimination between them is now presented in the sixteenth chapter.
It was stated in the previous chapter: "O Bhārata, having understood this, one becomes wise and has fulfilled all duties.
In that regard, who understands this reality, and who does not?

In response to this inquiry, the sixteenth chapter is commenced for the purpose of distinguishing between those who are qualified and those who are not qualified for the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*). For once the nature of the task (*kāryārtha*) has been established, there arises the desire to know who the qualified person (*adhikārin*) is.
As it was said by the Bhaṭṭas:
"When that by which a burden is to be carried has first been set in motion,
then it is possible to determine that 'Kaṇḍa is the carrier.
In this regard, he describes the divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*) which serves as a qualification for the eligible person (*adhikārī*) through three verses beginning with "abhayam."
Fearlessness is the absence of fear. Purity of being is the perfect clarity of the mind. The yoga of knowledge is the firm establishment and final consummation in the means for self-knowledge.
Generosity (*dāna*) is the appropriate distribution of one's own food and other provisions;
self-restraint (*dama*) is the control of the external sense faculties;
sacrifice (*yajña*) consists of the *darśa*, *paurṇamāsa*, and other rites according to one's qualification.
Self-study (*svādhyāya*) consists of the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahma-yajña*) and so forth,
or the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*).
Austerity (*tapas*) refers to the physical and other types that will be described in the subsequent chapter.
Uprightness is the absence of crookedness. //1//
Furthermore, what is non-violence? Non-violence is the avoidance of harming others.
Truth is the speaking of things exactly as they have been perceived.
Absence of anger is the non-arising of agitation in the mind even when struck. Generosity is magnanimity. Peace is the cessation of mental activity.
Slander is the publicizing of another's faults in their absence;
abstaining from that is non-slander. Compassion is sympathy toward living beings who are miserable.

Non-covetousness (*alolupatā*) is the state of not being covetous, the absence of greed; the elision of the vowel *a* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). Gentleness (*mārdava*) is softness, the quality of being non-cruel.
*Hrī* (modesty) is the sense of shame regarding the world in the undertaking of what should not be done;
*acapalatva* (steadfastness) is the absence of engagement in futile actions. //2//
Furthermore, what is "splendor" (*tejas*)? Splendor is boldness. Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is the restraint of anger when insults and the like arise.
Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the stabilization of the mind when it is desponding due to suffering and other such afflictions. Purity (*śauca*) is external and internal cleanliness.
Non-malice (*adroha*) is the absence of the desire to harm.
Excessive pride (*atimānitā*) is the conceit of being overly worthy of honor in oneself;
the absence of that is non-excessive pride (*nātimānitā*).
These twenty-six types, beginning with fearlessness, belong to one who is born into the divine nature (*daivī saṃpat*).
The meaning is that these [qualities] arise for a person destined for future prosperity, who has been born with an orientation toward that sattvic wealth which is worthy of the gods. //3//
Madhusūdana:

In the chapter on the Imperishable (Anantara), at the verse beginning "And its roots extend downwards, connected with actions in the world of men" (Gītā 15.2), the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) manifested in the human body according to the karma of previous births are stated to be the intermediate root of *saṃsāra*.

And these dispositions (*prakṛti*) of living beings—namely the divine (*daivī*), the demonic (*āsuri*), and the rakshasa (*rākṣasī*)—were indicated in the ninth chapter. Among them, the divine disposition is said to be the auspicious latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the nature of *sattva*, which is the cause for engaging in the performance of the means to self-knowledge as taught by the Vedas. Similarly, the demonic and rakshasa dispositions are the inauspicious latent impressions of the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are the causes for engaging in all manner of harmful actions that follow naturally established passion and hatred while transgressing Vedic prohibitions.
And it is called *prakṛti*.

In that regard, the distinction is as follows: due to the predominance of attachment (*rāga*) through the primary pursuit of sensual enjoyment, there is the state of an *āsuri*; and due to the predominance of hatred (*dveṣa*) through the primary pursuit of violence, there is the state of a *rākṣasī*.
However, at present, according to the scriptures, it is the *sāttvikī* [nature], which serves as the cause for engaging in the activities prescribed therein.

Pure latent impressions (*śubha-vāsanā*) constitute divine prosperity (*daivī saṃpat*). Impure latent impressions (*aśubha-vāsanā*), which arise from transgressing the scriptures and serve as the cause for engaging in those activities forbidden by them—whether characterized by passion (*rājasī*) or darkness (*tāmasī*)—constitute demonic prosperity (*āsuryā saṃpat*), through the unification of the *rākṣasa* and *āsura* types. Thus, the division of latent impressions into two categories is twofold: pure and impure.

The sixteenth chapter is commenced to establish, for the sake of acquiring the auspicious and abandoning the inauspicious, that which is well-known from such scriptural passages as, "Of Prajāpati there were two classes, the gods and the asuras," and so forth.
Therein, first, by means of three verses, [the Blessed One describes] the divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*) which is to be acquired.

Non-fear (*abhaya*) is either the state of being intent upon the practice of the meaning taught in the scriptures without doubt, or the absence of fear such as "How shall I live alone, devoid of all possessions?

Purity of being (*sattva-saṃśuddhi*) is the stainlessness of the internal organ (*sattva*); its perfection is the fitness for the manifestation of the reality of the Blessed One, or it is the avoidance of deceiving others, illusion, falsehood, and so forth.
Subjugating another through a pretext is deceiving another;
concealing one thing in the heart while acting otherwise outwardly is *māyā* (deception);
and speaking of something as seen in one way when it was otherwise is *anṛta* (falsehood), and so forth.
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the comprehension of the reality of the self (*ātma-tattva*) from the scriptures;

yoga is its being mounted upon one's own direct experience through one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). The "establishment in knowledge and yoga" (*jñāna-yoga-vyavasthiti*) is the constant abiding in those two, the perpetual dedication to them.
When, however, there is fearlessness— the maintenance of the resolve to grant safety to all beings—
this is also an indicative mark of other duties of the Paramahaṃsa,
such as the purification of one's being (sattva-saṃśuddhi).
Through the ripening of hearing and the other [limbs of yoga], the internal organ becomes free from the impurities of doubt, misconception, and the like.
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the direct realization of the Self (*ātma-sākṣātkāra*).

Yoga is the human effort conducive to the dissolution of the mind and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*). The state distinguished by these two is a condition distinct from that of the transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*).

When "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*) is explained as being established in the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), then this divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*) should be regarded as the very embodiment of its fruit;
for since the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇasaṃśuddhi*) is impossible without devotion to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavadbhakti*), that [purification] is also described by means of it.
But the great-souled ones, O Pārtha, taking refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undivided minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings. 13.

Thus, because divine prosperity (*daivī sampad*) has been described as consisting of devotion to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavad-bhakti*) in the ninth chapter, it should be understood that it was not listed alongside fearlessness and the other qualities due to its supreme excellence. Having described the divine prosperity— which is the fruit for the highly fortunate *paramahaṃsas*— [the text now proceeds] to those who are inferior to them, such as householders and others.

He explains that which constitutes the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*): giving (*dāna*) is the distribution, according to one's capacity, of food and other things over which one has ownership, as prescribed by the scriptures;
self-restraint (*dama*) is the control of the external senses, consisting in the absence of sexual intercourse and so forth at times other than the proper season for conception;
and the word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the unmentioned duties characterized by abstention (*nivṛtti*).
Sacrifice (*yajña*) consists of both that which is based on revelation (*śrauta*), such as the *agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and so forth,

and that which is based on tradition (*smārta*), namely the fourfold sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to beings, and the sacrifice to humans; for the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) is mentioned separately by means of the term "private Vedic study" (*svādhyāya*).
The particle *ca* serves to include other dharmas characterized by active engagement that have not been explicitly mentioned.
These three pertain to the householder.
*Svādhyāya* is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahma-yajña*), consisting of the study of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Although the term "yajña" (sacrifice) could include the mention of the fivefold great sacrifices, it is mentioned separately here for the purpose of describing it specifically as a duty of the religious student (*brahmacārin*).
Austerity (*tapas*)— of three kinds, such as bodily austerity and so forth, as will be described in the seventeenth chapter— is the specific duty of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).

Having thus stated the specific duties (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) of the four stages of life (*āśrama*), he now states the specific duties of the four social classes (*varṇa*): uprightness (*ārjava*) is the absence of crookedness; non-concealment of the knowledge one possesses regarding those listeners who are full of faith; non-injury (*ahiṃsā*) is the absence of the cause of injury, where injury (*hiṃsā*) is the cutting off of the livelihood of living beings;
and truth (*satya*) is speech that corresponds to reality and is not followed by harmful consequences.
Non-anger (akrodha) is the immediate pacification of that anger which arises when others have uttered insults or inflicted blows.

Renunciation (tyāga) is the giving away [of wealth], as previously mentioned. Tranquility (śānti) is the calming of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), as previously mentioned under self-restraint (dama).
Slander (*paiśuna*) is the disclosure of another's faults when that person is absent;
its absence is non-slander (*apaiśuna*).
Compassion (*dayā*) is sympathy toward suffering beings.

Non-covetousness (*aloluptva*) is the state of being free from longing; it is the absence of mental agitation even when the sense organs are in proximity to their objects. Gentleness (*mārdava*) is the absence of cruelty; it is the quality of instructing disciples and others without using harsh speech or the like, even toward those who raise frivolous objections.
Modesty (*hrī*) is a sense of social shame that acts as a restraint against the commencement of engaging in improper actions.
Lack of fickleness (*acāpalam*) is the absence of fickleness, which is the tendency to engage in activities of speech, hands, and so forth even without a purpose.
Qualities beginning with straightforwardness (*ārjava*) and ending with lack of fickleness are the unique duties (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) of a Brāhmaṇa. //2//

*Tejas* (splendor) is the state of being unassailable by the foolish, such as women and children; it is boldness. *Kṣamā* (forbearance) is the non-arising of anger toward one who causes insult, even when one possesses the capacity for retaliation. *Dhṛti* (fortitude) is a specific effort that sustains the body and the senses even when they have reached a state of exhaustion.
By means of which the faculties are uplifted and the body does not sink;

these three are unique to the Kṣatriya. Here, "purity" (śauca) refers to internal purity—the absence of deceit, falsehood, and so forth in the employment of wealth and other matters—and not external purity produced by earth, water, and the like. For the latter, being of the nature of bodily cleanliness, is external and lacks the quality of being an impression (*vāsanā*) within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

This is because it is precisely those latent impressions (*vāsanā*), distinguished by the divisions of *sāttvika* and so forth, that are intended here to be presented in the form of the divine and demoniacal endowments (*sampad*).
If they exist in the form of latent impressions through some aspect—just like Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and other such practices—that too is certainly to be accepted.
*Droha* is the grasping of weapons and so forth with the intent to kill another; the absence of that is *adroha*.
These two qualities are unique to the Vaiśya:

*mānitā*, which is the state of being honored, consisting of the intense cultivation of the feeling of one's own worthiness for respect; and *atimānitā*, which is the excellence of that feeling of being worthy of honor.
The absence of that is non-conceit, which is humility toward those worthy of honor.
This is the specific duty of the Śūdra.
Regarding this very [duty], the Brāhmaṇas seek to know [Brahman] through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting (BAU 4.4.22).

By such scriptural passages, both the specific and general duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), which are enjoined as being conducive to the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), are indicated here.

These duties come about—that is, they are accomplished—for a person born at the time of the commencement of a body, with reference to that divine wealth consisting of pure *sattva*, namely the continuum of latent impressions (*vāsanā-santati*) manifested by meritorious deeds. For such a person, knowledge and action [are required].

[The two follow him]: "both his former wisdom and his past deeds" (BAU 4.4.2), and "he becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action" (BAU 4.4.5); such are the scriptural passages.
By addressing him as "O Bhārata," he indicates that because you are born of a pure lineage and are thus purified, you are fit for such dharma. //3//
Viśvanātha:
In the sixteenth chapter, the Lord described divine and demoniac prosperity,
as well as the two-fold creation— divine and demoniac— from the Imperishable One.

Recalling that the fruits of the tree of worldly existence— which was described in the preceding chapter with the words "with roots above and branches below," and so forth— were not described, the Lord, intending to describe its two kinds of fruits in this chapter— namely, those that lead to liberation and those that cause bondage—
first speaks of the fruits of liberation in three verses beginning with "Fearlessness."
*Abhaya* (fearlessness) is the absence of fear regarding how one will live alone in a desolate forest after having abandoned sons, wife, and so forth.

*Sattva-saṃśuddhi* (purity of being) is clarity of mind. *Jñāna-yoga* is the means of knowledge; *vyavasthiti* (firm establishment) therein refers to the final perfection in such qualities as humility (*amānitva*) and the rest.
Generosity (dāna) is the appropriate sharing of one's own food and other possessions;
self-restraint (dama) is the control of the external sense faculties;
and sacrifice (yajña) is the worship of the gods.
Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the recitation of the Vedas;
the initial terms are clear. Renunciation (*tyāga*) is the relinquishing of self-restraint (*yamatā*) with regard to one's sons, wife, and so forth.
Freedom from greed is the absence of covetousness.

These twenty-six qualities, beginning with fearlessness, belong to a person who has attained birth at a moment that manifests the attainment of divine, sattvic prosperity—that is, one born with a view toward divine, sattvic wealth. (1–3)
Baladeva:
In the sixteenth [chapter], Kṛṣṇa spoke of the divine and demoniacal natures,
making known respectively the qualities to be accepted and those to be rejected.

In the preceding section, by the words "the roots of the aśvattha tree are intertwined," etc., the auspicious and inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanās*) caused by past actions were described as the intermediate roots of the tree of *saṃsāra*.
These very same impressions are designated in the ninth chapter as the divine (*daivī*), demoniacal (*āsurī*), and rakshasa (*rākṣasī*) natures of living beings.
Among these, the divine nature is the auspicious latent impression characterized by the performance of Vedic duties, which serves as the means for liberation.
That very divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*) is the fruit of the tree to be accepted here.

On the other hand, the impure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that follow natural passion and hatred—being *rājasa* and *tāmasa*, they are the cause of all misfortune—and the demonic and fiendish natures (*prakṛti*), which lead to a fall into hell: these constitute the fruit to be rejected by those two demonic endowments. It is to make this known that the sixteenth chapter begins.
In this context, the Blessed One spoke of divine endowment with the triad beginning with "fearlessness.
Here, the duties of the four stages of life (*āśrama*) and the social classes (*varṇa*) are described in succession.
First, regarding the renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), he says "fearlessness," which is the state of being devoid of fear such as, "How shall I live alone without effort?"
Purification of being (*sattva-saṃśuddhi*) is the clarity of the mind through the performance of the duties of one's own stage of life (*svāśrama-dharma*).

Steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), that is, in the means of knowledge such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, is the final consummation (*pariniṣṭhā*). These three constitute [the path].

Then he speaks regarding the students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*): "Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahma-yajña*)," meaning that one should be devoted to the practice of the Vedas with the realization that "this collection of syllables is the impersonal (*apauruṣeya*) revealer of the Blessed Lord who possesses all powers"—this is the first [duty]. Then he speaks regarding the forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*): "Austerity (*tapas*)."
And that [quality] consists of three types beginning with the body, as will be explained in the eighteenth chapter; this is the first [point].
Now, regarding the castes, he speaks of the Brahmins: "straightforwardness" (ārjava) means sincerity. And that should be understood as not concealing one's own knowledge from faithful listeners.

Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the non-destruction of the livelihood of living beings. Truth (*satya*) is speech concerning an object as it has been perceived, which does not entail harm. Absence of anger (*akrodha*) is the restraint of rising anger when one is insulted by a wicked person.
Renunciation is the avoidance of even ill-spoken words;
tranquility is the restraint of the mind;
and absence of backbiting is the non-disclosure of words that would cause harm to others behind their backs.
Compassion toward living beings is the inability to endure their suffering.
Freedom from greed is the absence of covetousness;
the elision of the letter *pa* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
Gentleness is softness; it is the inability to endure separation from association with worthy recipients. Modesty is shame regarding improper action.
Lack of fickleness is the absence of useless activity—these are the twelve.
Now he speaks of the qualities of the Kṣatriyas: *tejas* (splendor) is the state of being invincible by base people;
*kṣamā* (forbearance) is the absence of anger toward one who treats them with contempt, even when they have the capacity to retaliate;
and *dhṛti* (fortitude) is the effort that sustains the body and the senses so that they do not succumb to exhaustion—these three.
Now he speaks of the duties for Vaiśyas: purity consists in being free from deceit, fraud, and the like in their occupation or trade;
and non-malice consists in not taking up swords or other weapons with the intent to kill others—these two constitute the pair.

Then he speaks of the duties for Śūdras: lack of excessive pride, which is the absence of any sense of personal superiority, and humility toward the three classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—this is the single [duty]. Thus, there are twenty-six [duties in total].
These should be understood as the primary factors in their respective contexts, serving as indicators for those not explicitly mentioned.

They arise and manifest for a person born with auspicious divine latent impressions (*śubha-vāsanā*) made evident by meritorious deeds directed toward the commencement of a new body—according to the Vedic revelation: "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action."

Indeed, the gods are by nature devoted to following the Supreme Lord; this is their perfection, for through it arises the knowledge and devotion that lead to Him—this being the fruit to be accepted from the tree of worldly existence. (1-3)
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance— these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demonic nature. (16.4)
Śrīdhara says: He describes the demonic endowment with the word "hypocrisy" (dambha). Hypocrisy is the flaunting of religious virtue as a banner.
Arrogance (darpa) is the inflation of the mind caused by wealth, learning, and so forth.
Arrogance is as previously described;
so too is anger,
and harshness itself, which is to say, harsh speech.
Just as one with sight [perceives] the one-eyed, the one with form [perceives] the deformed, and one of noble birth [perceives] the one of low birth, and so forth;
and ignorance is non-discriminative knowledge, a false cognition regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and so on.
O Pārtha, for one who is "born" (abhijātasya), what is it to be "born" (abhijātasya)?
He said: "The wealth of the Asuras is 'Asurī';
the meaning is that it belongs to one who is born into that [nature]. //4//
Madhusūdana:
Having described the divine nature as that which is to be accepted, he now briefly describes the demonic nature as that which is to be rejected in a single verse, beginning with "Dambha.
Dambha is the desire for self-proclamation through hypocrisy; it is precisely this that constitutes being a "flag-waver" of righteousness (*dharma-dhvajitva*).
*Darpa* is a particular form of pride (*garva*) caused by wealth, kinsmen, and so forth, which serves as the cause for great contempt [for others].
*Atimāna* is the superimposition of an excessive degree of worthiness upon oneself.
Then both the gods and the asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, contended; thereupon, the asuras, through sheer *atimāna*, [fell] into whom...?
Thinking, "Now let us offer oblations," they proceeded offering in their own mouths; however, through excessive pride (*atimāna*) alone, they perished.
Therefore, one should not be arrogant, for it is said in the *Śatapatha-śruti*: "Excessive pride is indeed the gateway to ruin.

Furthermore, anger (*krodha*) is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti-viśeṣa*), characterized by a blazing nature and serving as the cause for the impulse to harm oneself or others.
Harshness (*pāruṣya*) is the habit of speaking with direct rudeness.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include other unmentioned faults that have become habitual, such as fickleness (*cāpalya*) and so forth.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the absence of discrimination regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and so on.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include other unmentioned defects such as lack of fortitude and so forth, which are of the nature of non-existence.

With reference to the demonic (*āsūrī*) attainment— which is characterized by passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), which causes delight to the demons, which consists of a continuous stream of inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
and which is manifested by sinful actions at the time of the body's inception— the hypocrisy and other [faults] of the base man who has been born [therein] [are described].

The meaning is that only defects such as ignorance exist, and not virtues such as fearlessness. By addressing him as "O Pārtha," He indicates his unfitness for such virtues due to his having a pure maternal lineage. //4//
Viśvanātha:
He states the fruits that act as bonds: *dambha* (hypocrisy) is the proclaiming of one's own righteousness even while being unrighteous;
*darpa* (arrogance) is pride or conceit caused by wealth, learning, and so forth, or the desire for honor from others, or attachment to wife, children, and the like.
Anger is well known;
harshness is cruelty;
ignorance is lack of discernment.

The term "demoniacal" (*āsurī*) is an illustration; the meaning is that these qualities, such as hypocrisy and the like, belong to a person who has obtained birth—that is, one who has acquired a moment indicative of the attainment of a demonic, rakshasa-like, or even tamasic disposition. //4//
Baladeva: Now, with one verse beginning with "Dambha," he describes the demoniac nature which is the cause of hell.
*Dambha* is the performance of religious duties for the sake of gaining a reputation for piety;
*darpa* is the pride born of learning and noble birth.
The notion of being worthy of worship directed toward oneself; anger is well known;
and harshness is the speaking of words that are perceptibly rough.
The letter *ca* (and) is a conjunctive particle for restlessness and the like.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the state of being devoid of the discernment between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
The [second] *ca* is a conjunctive particle for lack of fortitude and the like.
These [qualities] arise for a person born with manifest demonic propensities and inauspicious latent impressions (vāsanā) caused by misdeeds directed toward the commencement of a new body;
for such is the Vedic revelation: "One becomes sinful through sin. (4)
The divine nature is deemed to lead to liberation, while the demonic leads to bondage.
Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava, for you are born with a divine nature. 5.
Śrīdhara: Showing the function of these two types of fortune, he says, "The divine... The meaning is: one endowed with the divine fortune is qualified for the knowledge of reality taught by Me;
however, one endowed with the demoniacal fortune is eternally subject to transmigratory existence.

Having heard this, Arjuna—his mind agitated by the doubt of whether or not he was qualified for this—was comforted [by the Lord]: "O Pāṇḍava, do not grieve; do not give way to sorrow, because you are born with a divine nature. (5)
Madhusūdana:
The division of the fruits of these two types of prosperity is now stated in the verse beginning with "The divine" (daivī).
Whatever action is prescribed for a particular caste or stage of life that is characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and is free from attachment to results—that is [the divine prosperity].

His divine endowment— consisting of purity of being, devotion to the Blessed Lord, and culminating in the steady state of the yoga of knowledge— leads to liberation from the bondage of saṃsāra and to absolute isolation (kaivalya).
Therefore, that alone should be pursued by those seeking the highest good.

However, whatever action is prohibited by the scriptures, preceded by a desire for results, and accompanied by egoism—whether it be rajasic or tamasic—that entire action belongs to one who possesses the demonic nature (*āsuri sampat*).
Therefore, even the rakshasa-nature is included within that.
This [demonic nature] is considered and agreed upon by the scriptures and those who follow them to lead inevitably to bondage—that is, to the bondage of saṃsāra.
Therefore, the meaning is that this [ignorance] must indeed be abandoned by those seeking the highest good.
In this regard, the Blessed One consoles Arjuna, who is doubting with the thought "With what kind of perfection am I endowed?", saying:
"Do not grieve."
"Do not experience grief or remorse out of the fear that you are possessed of a demonic nature (*āsuryā saṃpat*).

You have been born with a divine nature (*daivī saṃpat*) as your aim; you are one who has acquired merit in the past and will possess merit in the future, O Pāṇḍava. The meaning is this: since the divine nature is well-known even among the other sons of Pāṇḍu, how much more so in your case? //5//
Viśvanātha:
He shows the function of these two types of wealth with the words "The divine... and so forth.

To Arjuna, who was distressed, thinking, "Alas, alas! This is my own asuric wealth—characterized by harshness, anger, and the like—which seeks to kill my kinsmen with arrows and leads to bondage in *saṃsāra*," [the Lord speaks].
He comforts me, saying, "Do not grieve.
O Pāṇḍava, for one born of a Kṣatriya lineage such as you, harshness, anger, and the like are indeed ordained by the treatises on Dharma in the context of battle;
the implication is that those qualities, such as violence and so forth, belong to the demonic nature (āsuri-sampat) only when directed elsewhere. //5//
Baladeva: With the half-verse beginning "The divine... (daivī), He clearly explains the difference in the fruits of these two types of wealth (*sampad*).

Observing Arjuna grieving—thinking, "This demonic wealth (*āsuri sampat*) of mine, characterized by harshness and anger as I desire to strike Droṇa and others with a rain of arrows, will lead me to hell"—He says, "Do not grieve" (*mā śucaḥ*).

O Pāṇḍava, since for you, a Kṣatriya, the discharge of arrows and such harshness in battle is ordained, this is indeed divine wealth; it is demonic only elsewhere. Therefore, do not grieve; do not give way to sorrow.
There are two types of created beings in this world: the divine and the demonic.
The divine has been described at length; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demonic. (16.6)
Śrīdhara: In order to show that the demonic nature (*āsuri saṃpat*) must be avoided with all one's being, he says "two" in order to elaborate upon that demonic nature.
"Two" means two kinds of creations of beings; hear them from my true words.
The word "two" is used by combining the demonic and the rakshasa natures into one.

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the threefold classification of *prakṛti* (nature) taught in the ninth chapter, beginning with the words, "having resorted to the delusive nature of the Rākṣasas and the Asuras," and so forth.
The rest is clear. //6//
Madhusūdana:

Now, let it be that the *rākṣasī* nature is included within the *āsuri* nature, since they are similar in their tendency toward actions prohibited by the scriptures; yet, because of the predominance of the enjoyment of desire and the predominance of violence toward living beings, it is appropriate to designate them as distinct in certain respects.

The third nature, however, is that of humans; it exists separately as the three classes of Prajāpati’s progeny—gods, humans, and asuras—who lived their period of studentship under their father Prajāpati (BAU 5.2.1).
Therefore, one might ask whether this [human nature] should be categorized among things to be abandoned or among things to be accepted; to this, he says: "Two.
In this world, throughout the entire path of transmigratory existence, there are only two kinds of creations of beings and two kinds of human creations.
The meaning is that there are only two types of creation, the divine (*daiva*) and the demonic (*āsura*), but there is no higher creation such as the *rākṣasa* or the *mānuṣa*.

Whenever a human being, through the power of refinement by the scriptures, overcomes the passion and hatred inherent in his own nature and becomes devoted to righteousness (*dharma*), he is then "divine."

But when, due to the intensity of innate passion and hatred, one overcomes the refinement of the scriptures and becomes devoted to unrighteousness (*adharma*), he is then an *asura*; for this twofold classification is logically established.
Indeed, there is no third category apart from righteousness (*dharma*) and unrighteousness (*adharma*).
Thus it is heard in scripture: "The offspring of Prajāpati were twofold: the gods and the asuras."
Then the gods, being the younger, and the Asuras, the elder, contended for these worlds.
Those gods said, "Come, let us overcome the Asuras in the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha" (BAU 1.3.1).

However, in a passage primarily concerned with the rules of self-restraint (*dama*), charity (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*)—such as the one beginning with "the three sons of Prajāpati"—it is understood that humans are those devoid of such self-restraint, charity, and compassion.

Since those who are actually *asuras* are metaphorically designated as "gods" (*devas*) or "humans" (*manuṣyas*) due to some commonality of characteristics, there is no room for [the claim of] superiority.
By means of the single syllable "da," Prajāpati gave instruction on self-restraint (*dama*) to humans who lack self-restraint,
and instruction on giving (*dāna*) to those who lack giving.
The instruction on compassion is directed toward those who lack it;
however, "those of a different kind" (vijātīya) here does not refer exclusively to gods, asuras, and humans, because this scripture has human beings as its intended audience.
Thus, at the conclusion, he summarizes: "This very same divine voice, the thunder, repeats: 'da-da-da'—meaning, 'Be self-controlled, give, be compassionate.'"
"One should train in these three: self-control, charity, and compassion" (BAU 5.2.3).
Therefore, it is rightly said that "there are two types of creation of beings," since both the demonic (*rākṣasa*) and human (*mānuṣa*) natures are included within the demonic (*āsura*) nature.
Among those, the divine creation of beings has been described by me to you in detail, through various modes of elaboration, in the context of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established.

In the second [chapter], the characteristics of the devotees; in the twelfth, the characteristics of knowledge; and in the thirteenth, the characteristics of one who has transcended the qualities, by means of the passage beginning with "and here there is fearlessness" (13.1).

Now, listen to my detailed exposition of the demonic creation of beings through my words; comprehend it thoroughly for the sake of its abandonment, for only when it is correctly known can it be avoided.
"In order to act"—by indicating the connection with "O Pārtha," he shows that [this matter] is not to be neglected. //6//
Viśvanātha:

Furthermore, in order to elaborate upon the demonic endowment (*āsurī saṃpat*) for the sake of Arjuna who was thus despondent, He says, "Two [types of people]," referring to the passage beginning with "Fearlessness, purity of being," and so forth. //6//
Baladeva: Nevertheless, observing that his grief has not ceased, [the Lord] elaborates upon the demonic nature [of Arjuna] by saying "two.
In this human world, which is the locus for the performance of ritual action (*karma-adhikārin*), there are two kinds of creation of beings—that is, two types of human creations.
When this person, having cast off natural attachment and aversion in the human world through the scriptures, becomes a performer of scriptural duties, then he is divine.
When one abandons the scripture and, being subject to natural passion and aversion, practices unscriptural duties, then he is demonic;
for there is indeed no third category other than dharma and adharma.
And the Śruti says thus: "There were two classes of Prajāpati’s offspring, the gods and the asuras," and so forth (BAU 1.3.1).
Therein, the divine path has been described in detail with the words beginning "fearlessness.
Now hear about the demonic; I shall describe it in detail. //6//
Asuras do not understand either the path of action or the path of renunciation; in them neither purity nor right conduct nor truth is found. (16.7)
Śrīdhara: He describes the demonic nature in detail through twelve verses beginning with "pravṛttiṃ ca" (and their engagement).
People of demonic nature do not know engagement in dharma nor withdrawal from adharma;
therefore, purity, right conduct, and truthfulness simply do not exist in them. //7//
Madhusūdana:

[The Lord] explains the demoniac nature (*āsurī saṃpat*)—which was to be avoided—as a qualification of those living beings, in the twelve verses preceding this one. By the word "pravṛtti," he means both the path of action (*pravṛtti*) and, by the force of the word "ca" (and), the duty (*dharma*) that is its object, as well as the prohibitory statements that enjoin it; people of demoniac nature do not know these.
Therefore, for them, neither the two kinds of purity nor the conduct (*ācāra*) taught by Manu and others exists,
nor does truthfulness— defined as speaking what is pleasant, beneficial, and true— exist.
Although purity and truthfulness are included within conduct, they are mentioned separately according to the maxim of the "Brahmin and the Wandering Mendicant" (*brāhmaṇa-parivrājaka-nyāya*).
For those who are impure, lacking in good conduct, speakers of untruth, deceitful, and demonic are well known. //7//
Viśvanātha:
Engagement in dharma and withdrawal from adharma. //7//
Baladeva: With twelve verses, he describes the demonic creation and its active engagement (*pravṛtti*).
Demonic people do not know how to engage in dharma nor how to desist from adharma;
by the two uses of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that they also do not know the injunctions and prohibitions—the scriptural statements—that establish those two.
It has been stated that this is because they lack faith in the Vedas.
In those [scriptures], neither the external and internal purity conducive to their practice nor the conduct prescribed by Manu and others exists.

And truthfulness does not necessarily entail the welfare of living beings, as in the case of statements concerning objects exactly as they are perceived; therefore, their teaching and so forth are like those of vultures and jackals. //7//
They say that this world is without truth, without a foundation, and without a Lord; it has arisen from mutual union, caused by nothing other than desire. (16.8)
Śrīdhara: But how is it that they do not know the engagement in and withdrawal from dharma and adharma as declared by the Vedas?
Or, in the absence of accepting dharma and adharma, how could there be the established order of pleasure, pain, and so forth in the world?
Furthermore, how could they transgress the commands of the Lord regarding matters such as purity and conduct?
And if God is not accepted, from what could the origin of the world arise?
Therefore, he says: "unreal" (*asatya*). They say that the world is such that there exists no truth—such as the authority of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and so forth—in it.
The meaning is that they do not accept the authority of the Vedas and so forth.
As it has been said: "The authors of the Veda are three: a rogue, a deceiver, and a night-stalker," and so on.

Therefore, the meaning is that they say the diversity of the world is inherent (*svābhāvika*), such that it has no basis or cause for its regulation in the form of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). For this very reason, they say the world is such that there is no Lord (*īśvara*) who acts as its creator and regulator.
If so, from what [source] do they say this world originates?
To this he says: "arisen from mutual dependence" (*aparasparasambhūtam*). *Aparaspara* means "the other and the other."
The world has arisen from the union of male and female, through mutual interaction and not otherwise;
what else could it be?
There is no other cause for this whatsoever;
rather, it is caused solely by desire.
The meaning is that they say the cause of this is precisely desire, which exists in the form of a continuous flow between both women and men. //8//
Madhusūdana:

Now, there exists the authoritative means of knowledge known as the Veda, which is faultless, consists of the command of the Blessed Lord, and is renowned throughout all the worlds; it teaches the engagement in and desisting from action regarding dharma and adharma, and there exist the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth, which depend upon it.

How, then, can there be ignorance regarding the engagement [in dharma], its cessation, and the means of knowledge for them? Or, even if there is knowledge, how could there be a state of lacking purity, conduct, and so forth among the wicked due to their non-performance [of dharma] while the Blessed One—the punisher of those who transgress against what is known—exists? For the Blessed One, as the punisher, is well-known in both the world and the Vedas. To this, he says: "Untrue."
The Veda—known as the authority that reveals reality—is true insofar as its intended meaning is uncontradicted; likewise, the Purāṇas and other texts dependent upon it are true.

There is no such thing where these are untrue. Although the very nature of the Veda is established by perception, its validity is not accepted [by the opponent], and thus there is an absence of that specific quality. For this very reason, it is "unfounded" (*apratiṣṭha*), meaning it lacks a firmly established basis for determining what constitutes merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Likewise, they say that the world is without a Lord— that is, it lacks a sovereign controller who bestows the fruits of good and evil actions;
those Asuras maintain this view because, due to the obstruction posed by powerful evil, they do not acknowledge the authority of the Veda.

And consequently, since they do not accept dharma and adharma as understood through that [scripture], nor the Lord (Īśvara), they fall away from the goals of human life by acting according to their own whims; this is the meaning.

Anticipating the objection—"If the world is held to be devoid of the Supreme Lord, who presides over primordial nature (prakṛti) with the aid of dharma and adharma known solely through scripture, how can it arise in the absence of a cause?"—he says: "arisen from mutual interaction" (aparaspara-sambhūtam).
The world, produced from the mutual union of men and women engaged in desire, has desire as its cause; it has desire alone as its cause, being devoid of any cause other than desire.
[Objection: But are not dharma and other factors also causes?
"No," he says; what else?
Is there any other unseen cause? The meaning is that there is none at all.

Even if one accepts the unseen (adṛṣṭa), since it must ultimately resolve into some inherent nature (svabhāva) upon reaching its limit, let the diversity of the world be merely natural (svābhāvika); for when the visible is possible, there is no room for the postulation of the unseen.
Therefore, they say that desire alone is the cause of living beings, and nothing else such as the unseen or a Lord (īśvara). This is the Lokāyata view. //8//
Viśvanātha:
He states the opinion of the Asuras: "They say that the world is unreal, false, and merely perceived through delusion;
it is unstable, being devoid of any foundation or support."
The meaning is that there is no substratum whatsoever for a sky-flower.
Because it is false, it is "without a Lord" (anīśvara), meaning it is not produced by a creator Lord.
Because beings such as those born from moisture arise spontaneously, they are "not produced from one another."
What more need be said?
"Caused by desire" (*kāmahaituka*) means that for proponents [of such views], desire itself is the cause;
because it is merely false, they assert "this is exactly as one can imagine it."
Others, however, explain it thus: "Asatya" means that there is no truth—that is, no authoritative source such as the Vedas or Purāṇas—in which [the doctrine] is found;
for it has been said: "The authors of the three Vedas are jesters, rogues, and night-stalkers," and so forth.
"Apratiṣṭham" means that there is no foundation—that is, no established order consisting of dharma and adharma—in which [the doctrine] is found.
The sense is that even *dharma* and *adharma* are perceived through delusion;
the sense is that even a non-Lord (*anīśvara*) is perceived as a Lord (*īśvara*) due to delusion.
Now, one might object: "This world is seen to have arisen from the specific mutual efforts of male and female."
The sense is that, just as the potter’s knowledge regarding the production of a jar is merely delusion, there is indeed no such knowledge in the parents regarding the production of such a child.
"What else? What else?"—the sense is: what more need be said?
Therefore, this world has desire as its cause; it is that wherein those who imagine causes [where none exist] have desire as their own-will alone as the cause.
The meaning is that those who, by the power of reasoning, are able to assert such things as atoms, illusion, or Īśvara, they declare that very thing to be its cause. //8//
Baladeva: He demonstrates their doctrines; therein, he states the view of those who maintain the doctrine of a single self (eka-jīva-vādins) with the words "asatyam" and so forth.
This world is unreal, a manifestation of delusion like [the appearance of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell;
it is unstable and without support, like a flower in the sky.
There is no such thing as a Lord who is the cause of birth and so forth;
even He, like that [world], is merely constructed by delusion.
If such a Lord were established as ultimately real, the world created by Him would not be something that appears and then vanishes almost immediately, just as it is observed to do.
Therefore, they consider the world to be unreal:

consciousness alone is without distinction and is not cognized by any means of valid knowledge; through the delusion of consciousness, there is one individual soul (*jīva*), and from that [consciousness], the other—consisting of the insentient, the individual souls, and the Lord—appears due to ignorance of it.
Until the direct realization of one's own true nature, this appears consistent [with experience], like elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth in a dream, until one wakes up.

And when there is the direct realization of one's true nature (*svarūpa-sākṣātkāra*), that which is imagined through ignorance regarding it would cease along with its state as an individual soul (*jīvatva*), just as the chariot, horses, and so forth in a dream cease in deep sleep.

Now, he addresses the Buddhists who maintain the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāva-vādin*): "Not produced from mutual [causes]" means that the world is not born from the sexual union of man and woman;
for just as a potter is required for the production of a jar, there is an absence of knowledge on the part of the father and others in the production of a child, even though they exist.
Because lineages arise repeatedly in sexual union, and because beings such as those born from sweat arise suddenly;
therefore, this [world] comes into being solely from its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Then, regarding the Lokāyatikas, he says: "It has desire as its cause."
What else remains to be said?
For a woman or a man, desire alone is the cause [of this state] by way of its continuous flow; thus, the suffix *ṭhañ* is used in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*).
Alternatively, according to the Jains, it means that desire is the cause [of this state] simply by its own will.
The meaning is that whatever one might be able to conceive by the power of reasoning, that very thing he declares to be its cause. //8//
Holding fast to this view, those of ruined souls and meager intellect, performing cruel deeds and hostile to the world, arise for its destruction. (9)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "relying on this":

relying upon this view or philosophy of the Lokāyatikas, those of ruined souls—meaning those with defiled minds—and of small intellect—meaning those whose thoughts consist of nothing but wicked purposes—become harmful enemies of the world; being such, they prevail for the destruction of the world, which means they arise [for that purpose]. (9)
Madhusūdana:
Anticipating the objection that this view might be accepted as being like a scriptural view, he says "etām" (this).
Having grasped—that is, having relied upon—this previously mentioned Lokāyatika view, those whose souls are ruined have lost the means for attaining the next world.

Those of small intellect, whose minds are occupied only with what is seen and with immediate instruction, who perform fierce deeds, who are harmful and enemies of the world—all such beings arise and manifest in the form of tigers, serpents, and so forth, for the destruction of the multitude of living creatures.
Therefore, because this view is the cause of an extremely low rebirth, it must be abandoned by all means by those who seek their own welfare; this is the meaning. //9//
Viśvanātha:

To those asuras who speak thus— some of whom have lost their self-control, some of whom possess little knowledge, and some of whom perform fierce deeds and act according to their own whims— he declares that they become inhabitants of the great hells,
by means of these eleven verses beginning with "etām."
Having firmly grasped; having taken as an object. //9//

Baladeva says: "By resorting to these philosophical systems (*darśana*), which were composed by them as determinations of their respective doctrines, the world perishes"—the word *etām* is used in the singular to denote the class [of systems].

Taking hold of and relying upon these systems, those of small intellect, whose self is lost—meaning they have not perceived the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth—and who are performers of fierce deeds, being devoted to actions such as violence, calumny, and harshness, become harmful enemies to the world.
They lead to destruction; the meaning is that they cause the world to fall away from the ultimate truth. //9//
Taking refuge in insatiable desire, possessed by hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance,
they act with impure vows, having grasped false notions through delusion. (16.10)

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having resorted to desire" (*kāmam āśritya*): having resorted to desire—which is difficult to satisfy (*duṣpūram*) and impossible to fulfill—they, being possessed by hypocrisy and other such traits, engage in the worship of inferior deities and the like.
How so?

Having embraced false notions—such as "By means of this mantra, having propitiated this deity, we shall attain great treasures"—they proceed by adopting such perverse attachments through mere delusion.
They are those whose vows are impure, meaning they possess vows that take impure objects such as liquor, meat, and so forth. (10)
Madhusūdana:
And when they, by some action or other, attain a human birth, then—
should they desire to fulfill that particular longing for perceived objects, which is difficult to satisfy and impossible to fulfill— they do so through hypocrisy and unrighteousness.

Furthermore, possessed of false attachments and inauspicious certainties— due to pride in proclaiming their own righteousness even when they are unworthy of honor, due to intoxication in proclaiming their own worthiness of honor even when they are not, and due to the superimposition of exceptional excellence even when they are devoid of it, which serves as a cause for great contempt—
they think: "Having propitiated this deity with this mantra, we shall perform the summoning of passionate women."

Having grasped this through delusion and lack of discrimination—consisting of such dogmatic attachments as "By propitiating this deity with this mantra, we shall attain great treasures"—and not from the scriptures, those who observe impure vows proceed toward any and every non-Vedic practice that yields visible results, such as the worship of minor deities;
the ellipsis is to be supplied as "they fall into an impure hell," which connects with the following verse. //10//
Viśvanātha:
Those of evil intellect proceed with false attachments;
they are those whose vows consist of impurities and are devoid of pure conduct. //10//

Baladeva: Now, he describes their wickedness and evil conduct with the words "kāmaṃ" (desire). Relying on desire—that is, thirst for sense objects—which is difficult to satisfy, and out of delusion rather than from the scriptures, they proceed while adopting impure vows.

They adopt "evil attachments"—that is, stubborn dogmas like predatory crocodiles that lead to one's own destruction—consisting of imaginary deities, their mantras, and the means of worshipping them, as well as the attraction of women, kings, and hidden treasures.
This is the meaning:
they are those whose vows consist of impure practices such as frequenting cemeteries, consuming liquor and meat, and indulging in the objects of the senses;

and who are possessed of hypocrisy—which is the pretense of being most righteous despite being devoid of righteousness—of pride—which is the pretense of being worthy of worship despite being unworthy of worship—and of intoxication—which is the attribution of superiority despite lacking excellence.
Resorting to immeasurable anxiety that ends only with death, they regard the gratification of desires as the supreme goal, being certain that "this is all. (16.11)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "what is the use of anxiety":
they have resorted to an immeasurable anxiety—that is, one whose end is dissolution, which is to say death—and thus cannot be measured;
the meaning is that they are constantly devoted to anxiety.
Those for whom the enjoyment of sensual pleasures alone is supreme;
that is to say, those who have reached the firm conviction that the enjoyment of sensual pleasures alone is the highest human goal and that there is nothing else.
"They strive for the accumulation of wealth"—this is the syntactical connection with what follows.
And thus there is a Bārhaspatya Sūtra: "Desire alone is the sole human goal," and "A person is desire characterized by consciousness. //11//
Madhusūdana further qualifies those very [sorrows] with the word "cintām" (thought):

thought consisting of the deliberation upon the means for one's own acquisition and preservation (*yoga-kṣema*), which is immeasurable because its objects are immeasurable, and which has dissolution—meaning death—as its end; that is, lasting as long as life.
The word "anuvartamānām" (following) means "as long as.
The particle "ca" has the sense of conjunction, indicating that not only do those of impure vows engage in such conduct, but they also rely upon such thoughts.
Although they are always intent on endless thoughts, they are never possessed of thoughts concerning the world beyond; rather, they are solely devoted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.

They are called "desires" (*kāma*) because they are desired; these are the perceived objects such as sound and so forth. For those for whom the enjoyment of these alone is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and not virtue (*dharma*) and the like, [the author] says this in response to the question of why they do not desire the highest happiness of the next world: "This much alone is happiness that is seen, and nothing else."
They are those who possess such a certainty, being convinced that "this is the pleasure to be enjoyed upon separation from the body, because there is no enjoyer distinct from this body.
And thus says the Bārhaspatya Sūtra: "The person (puruṣa) is the body qualified by consciousness."
And [the view that] "sensual pleasure alone is the sole aim of human life. //11//
Viśvanātha:

"Ending with dissolution" means ending with death—that is, reaching its limit. "Those for whom this alone is the purport of the scriptures" refers to those who have determined that the essential meaning of the treatises is merely this: "Let the senses plunge into the pleasures of sense objects; what concern is there? (11–15)

Baladeva: [Those who] have resorted to immeasurable, secondary thought—which concerns objects to be accomplished until the time of death and ends at the dissolution of the universe—for whom the enjoyment of desires, that is, the proper pursuit of sense-objects alone, is the supreme human goal;
for them, this alone, namely the mere enjoyment of desires, is the concern of this world (*aihika*).
Having reached the firm conviction that there is no happiness pertaining to the next world other than this, they remain steadfast. //11//
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope, devoted to desire and anger,
they strive for the accumulation of wealth through unjust means for the sake of enjoying their desires. 16.12
Śrīdhara: For this very reason, he says "by hopes. Hopes themselves are the bonds; bound by hundreds of them, they are dragged hither and thither.

Those who are devoted to desire and anger—those for whom desire and anger are their supreme resort—strive for, that is, they seek through unjust means such as theft, the accumulation and hoarding of wealth for the sake of enjoying sensual pleasures. //12//
Madhusūdana:

Such are those *asuras*; their desires and aspirations—whether directed toward objects for which there is no possible means or toward objects for which the means are unknown—are like snares because they are the cause of bondage. Bound, as it were, by hundreds of such collections of snares, they fall away from the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).

Then, being dragged away, those for whom desire and anger are the supreme resort or support— meaning those who are "devoted to desire and anger," which is to say, they are always gripped by the longing for sexual union with women and the longing for what is undesirable—
strive and exert themselves for the sake of sensual enjoyment and not for the sake of dharma, accumulating hoards of wealth through unjust means such as seizing the property of others.

By the use of the plural form "accumulations" (saṃcayān), it is shown that even when wealth is acquired, greed—characterized by an ever-increasing thirst for sense objects due to the persistence of that craving—is present. //12//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: "Āśā" (hope) is clear.
They "īhante," meaning they strive or endeavor through unjust means, such as false testimony and theft. //12//
"Today this has been gained by me; this desire I shall attain;
this is mine, and this wealth also shall be mine again. //13//
Śrīdhara: Speaking of their desire, he describes their attainment of hell with these four verses beginning with "This today by me.
*Prāpsye* means "I shall attain";
*manoratham* means "that which is dear to the mind."
The rest is clear.
And the connection with the fourth [verse] is that those who are deluded by ignorance regarding these three verses fall into hell. //13//
Madhusūdana explains their such persistence in the thirst for wealth by means of a description of their mental fantasies, saying "this":
"This wealth has been obtained by me today, now, through this particular means."
"I shall soon obtain this, which fulfills other desires and brings satisfaction to the mind;
this has already been accumulated and is in my house;
and even more wealth will come again in the coming year."
Thus, those agitated by thirst for wealth fall into the impure hell; this is the connection with what follows. //13//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Revealing their persistence in the hope for wealth through the expression of their mental fantasies, he describes their fall into hell with these four verses beginning with "idaṃ.
"This field, consisting of cattle, sons, and so forth, has been acquired by me today through the power of my own intellect."
"I myself shall attain this cherished desire and this object of my heart by my own power;
this wealth already acquired is now mine through my own power alone;
and this desired wealth shall belong to me next year solely by my own strength."

But it is not by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) nor by the grace of the Lord (īśvara); such is the meaning. Having thus elaborated upon the thirst for wealth, he now elaborates upon the wicked disposition: "This enemy named Yajñadatta has been slain by me, who am exceedingly powerful."
"I alone shall slay even other enemies, and I shall carry away their wives, wealth, and so forth"—by the word "and" (ca), the implication is that no one shall live by my hand.

Now, some say that the will of God (Īśvara) and unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa) are the causes of victory; to that he says: "I alone am the Lord (Īśvara), independent," meaning that I am naturally endowed with all enjoyments and am myself the enjoyer.
"I am the accomplished one.
If someone were to postulate an Īśvara, then let him postulate me alone as the Īśvara and not anyone other than me, because no such other is perceived; this is the intended meaning. //13//
"This enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well;
I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy. (16.14)
Śrīdhara: "This one" refers to the Siddha, one who has accomplished his task. The rest is clear. //14//
Madhusūdana,
having thus elaborated upon greed, elaborates upon their anger by stating its very intention with the words "asau" (this one):
"This enemy named Devadatta, who was exceedingly difficult to conquer, has been slain by me."

Therefore, now I shall kill him with ease; and I shall kill all other enemies as well—the sense of "api" (also/even) being that not even one shall remain alive by my hand. By the use of the word "ca" (and), the intention is that I shall not only kill them, but shall also seize their wives, wealth, and so forth.

From where does such power of yours come? It might be thought that it arises from the possibility of enemies who are your equals or even your superiors; therefore, he says: "I am the Lord (īśvara), not merely a human being, by which [status] there might be someone equal to me or superior to me.
What will these wretches do? In every way, there is no one equal to me. With this intention, he reveals his lordship.

For I am a possessor of enjoyments, endowed with all the requisites for pleasure; I am successful, provided with companions such as sons and servants; I am strong by nature, highly energetic, happy, and entirely free from disease. //14//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Nothing.
"I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, I shall rejoice"—thus are they deluded by ignorance. (15)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word "āḍhya":
one who is *āḍhya* is endowed with wealth and so forth;
one who is *abhijanavān* is of noble birth.
"By performing sacrifices and other rituals, I shall attain great prestige from others who are initiated;
I shall give gifts to those belonging to you;
I shall rejoice—I shall attain joy. Thus, deluded by ignorance, they have fallen into a false attachment. 15.
Madhusūdana:
[Objection: "But might someone be equal to him by virtue of wealth or lineage? To this he says, "the wealthy" (āḍhya); that is, one who possesses riches.
"I am indeed one who possesses noble lineage and am well-born;
therefore, the meaning is that there is no one else equal to me.
Thinking that someone might be his equal through yoga or through charity, he says: "I shall sacrifice," meaning I shall surpass others even by means of sacrifice.
"I shall give wealth to the panegyrists and the actors and so forth;

and thereafter I shall rejoice—I shall obtain delight—in the company of dancers and others. Thus, deluded by ignorance and lack of discernment, they have been led into various forms of delusion—a succession of errors. //15//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.

Baladeva: If it is objected, "Surely others are seen who are equal to you in wealth and lineage; how then can you be the Lord?", he says: "I am rich, endowed with prosperity, and by my very nature I am of noble birth—that is, I am well-born."
But there is no one else like me for any reason;
since there is no one at all, I alone am the Lord.
Therefore, by my power alone, I shall perform sacrifice and bring about union with celestial women.
"I shall give [them to you];
I will surely bite off their lips and so forth; I will delude them"—thus, being utterly bewildered by ignorance, they fall into hell; this is the connection with what follows.
Their minds are distracted and scattered among many objects that require long effort to achieve, and being enveloped by a net consisting of delusion, they are like fish unable to escape from it.
Those who are addicted to sensual pleasures, dying in their midst, fall into impure hells such as Vaitaraṇī and others. //15-16//
Perplexed by many thoughts, enveloped in the snare of delusion, and attached to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into an impure hell. (16.16)
Śrīdhara: Listen to what those who have become thus attain, beginning with the words "aneka-":
their minds are engaged in manifold desires; thus they are *anke-citta*.
By that [mind], they are bewildered and distracted.
Enveloped by that very net consisting of delusion,
like fish constrained by a net made of thread,
those who are thus attached to and obsessed with sensual pleasures fall into the impure and defiled hell. //16//
Madhusūdana:

They are variously deluded by many minds of the aforementioned types and by their respective evil intentions, because they are shrouded by the net of delusion (*moha*). Delusion is the incapacity to discriminate between what is beneficial and what is harmful; it is like a net because, being of the nature of an obstruction, it is a cause of bondage.
The meaning is that they are completely enveloped and entangled on all sides by that, like fish caught in a net made of thread, and thus brought under the control of another.

For this very reason, being addicted even to the enjoyment of desires—which are means for achieving what is undesirable to themselves—and being entirely devoted to those alone, their sins accumulate at every moment, and they fall into the foul Vaitaraṇī and other hells filled with excrement, urine, phlegm, and the like. //16//
Viśvanātha:
In the impure hell, such as Vaitaraṇī and others. //16//
Baladeva: Nothing.
Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride.
They perform what are called sacrifices through hypocrisy, contrary to the prescribed rules. //17//

Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "of those who wish to sacrifice," the intention is that the desire expressed by them is characterized solely by hypocrisy, egoism, and the like, and is not of the nature of *sattva*; thus he says with two verses, beginning with "by themselves":
they have been honored—that is, led to a state of respectability—by themselves alone, and not by any virtuous persons.
Therefore, they are stubborn and unbending.
Being possessed of both wealth and the intoxication of the mind,
those sacrifices which exist in name only are called "name-sacrifices."
Or else, they perform those sacrifices merely for the sake of gaining renown by such names as "initiated" or "performer of Soma-sacrifices";
how?
With hypocrisy.
But not with faith;
and it is performed in such a way that it is devoid of the prescribed ritual procedure. //17//
Madhusūdana:

[Objection: "But since it is observed that even some among them engage in Vedic rituals such as sacrifices and giving, their falling into hell is improper. [Reply: No; he says, "Self-conceited" (ātma-sambhāvitāḥ).
They are those who have been made to believe in their own worthiness—that they are distinguished by all virtues—by themselves alone, and not by any virtuous persons.
"Stiff" means unbending;
because they are possessed of the pride and intoxication caused by wealth— that pride which consists in the superimposition of an excessive sense of one's own worthiness upon oneself,
and that intoxication which consists in the conceit of being unworthy of honor even toward others such as gurus— they [perform] sacrifices in name only.

They sacrifice with sacrifices that are mere in name, not substantial— either sacrifices that merely produce titles such as "Soma-sacrificer" and the like, or sacrifices performed contrary to the rules, lacking the prescribed limbs and procedures, out of hypocrisy and the display of religious virtue, and not out of faith.
Therefore, the meaning is that they do not partake in the fruit thereof. //17//
Viśvanātha:
The meaning is that they have been honored—that is, led to a state of worshipfulness—by themselves alone, and not by any virtuous persons;
for this very reason, they are stiff and unbending.
Those sacrifices which exist by name alone are "name-sacrifices" (nāma-yajña); [it is] by means of them [that they are so characterized]. //17//
Baladeva: They have been made to esteem themselves and led to a state of superiority by their own selves, and not by virtuous people who know the scriptures;
they are stubborn and unbending.

They are possessed of intoxication and pride arising from wealth, prosperity, and honor—such as being called a *paramahaṃsa*, a great ascetic (*mahā-śramaṇa*), the venerable master (*śrī-pūjya-pāda*), or a performer of great worship (*mahā-pūjā-vid*). By means of "name-sacrifices"—that is, sacrifices consisting of mere names and ritual procedures for worship—they worship deities of their own invention for the sake of the worldly advancement of their respective householders. They are distinguished by hypocrisy and the flaunting of the banner of righteousness (*dharma-dhvajitva*);
the meaning is that they merely assume the appearance of those who are detached.
In such a way that it is contrary to the prescribed rule and not ordained by the Veda. //17//
Taking refuge in egoism, power, arrogance, lust, and anger, they hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, being full of envy. 16.18
Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon the very nature of performing rituals contrary to the prescribed rules with the words "egoism" (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth.
Being possessed by egoism and other such traits, they worship while hating Me—who am present in their own bodies and in the bodies of others as the conscious element (*cid-aṃśa*).
In sacrifices performed out of ostentation (*dambha-yajña*), because of the absence of faith, there is only the useless affliction of oneself.
Likewise, even in the case of animals and the like, when they are killed contrary to the prescribed rule, nothing remains but an injury to their consciousness; thus it is said that they "hate.
"Envious" (abhyasūyakāḥ) means those who attribute faults to the virtues of those who walk the path of the righteous. //18//
Madhusūdana:

For those of demoniac nature (*āsurāḥ*), who are engaged in actions such as sacrifice and charity with a resolve (*saṅkalpa*) characterized primarily by hypocrisy, egoism, and the like—thinking "I shall sacrifice" or "I shall give"—even their external means of accomplishment do not succeed; and their internal means, such as knowledge, dispassion, and devotion to the Lord, are utterly unattainable for them. This is what [the Lord] expresses in the verse beginning with "egoism."
I am the nature of self-conceit (*abhimāna*); that which is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is common to all.

However, through these superimposed qualities, one develops the conceit of greatness regarding oneself, which is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), as well as strength (*bala*)—the specific capacity residing in the body for the purpose of overcoming others—and pride (*darpa*)—which consists of the disdain for others and serves as the cause for transgressing against gurus, kings, and so forth.
They have resorted to specific defects of the mind—namely, desire, which is longing for desired objects; anger, which is aversion toward undesired objects;
and, by virtue of the word "and" (ca), envy, which consists in intolerance of the virtues of others—as well as other great defects.
If it be argued that even such fallen persons, being purified by devotion to you, will not fall into hell, he says "no":

because of the ripening of adverse fate, they fail to recognize Me—the Lord, the Blessed One—who exist as the witness of their respective cognitions and actions within the bodies of those Asuras and others, such as their sons and wives, which are the objects of their affection; though I am the supreme object of love, I am not perceived within those bodies.
Those who hate my command as the Lord— namely, the *śruti* and *smṛti*— are those who, by being averse to the performance of the duties prescribed therein, transgress them;
for it is well known in the world that such transgression of the commands of kings and others constitutes hatred toward them.

Now, one might ask: why do teachers and others not instruct them? To this he replies: they are envious (*abhyasūyakāḥ*), meaning they attribute faults such as deceit to the compassion and other virtues of their teachers who abide on the Vedic path.
Therefore, the meaning is that being devoid of all means of spiritual attainment, they fall into hell alone.

There is another explanation for the phrase "Me, in the bodies of oneself and others": [it refers to Me] existing in one's own bodies and in the bodies of others by way of the conscious element (*cid-aṃśa*).
Those who hate Me perform sacrifices out of hypocrisy; because of the absence of faith, there is suffering for themselves due to the vows of initiation and so forth.
Likewise, by the unrighteous slaughter of animals and other beings, nothing remains but an offense against consciousness.

According to another explanation, "those who hate Me" refers to those who, due to the delusion of [identifying with] humanity and so forth, harbor hatred toward Me—who have entered their own bodies as the living souls (jīvas) in the forms of the Lord’s pastimes known as Vāsudeva and others.
Likewise, the construction is: "They hate Me, who am eternally manifest within the bodies of others and within the bodies of My devotees, such as those known as Prahlāda and others.
For it is said in the Ninth Chapter:
"The deluded disregard Me when I have assumed a human form."
Not knowing my higher nature as the Great Lord of all beings.
"Vain are their hopes, vain their actions, vain their knowledge, and deluded their minds;

they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric. (Gītā 9.11–12) And elsewhere it is said: "The unintelligent think of me, who am unmanifest, as having come into manifestation. (Gītā 8.23)
And thus, because of hatred toward one worthy of worship, Pūtanā did not arise through devotion; this is the meaning. //18//
Viśvanātha:

[They are] those who, failing to honor Me, the Supreme Self, actually hate Me; or rather, those saintly persons who are devoted to the Self—that is, intent upon the Supreme Self—and who hate Me residing within their bodies. The underlying sense is that by hating the bodies of the saintly, they indeed hate Me.
Envious ones are those who attribute faults to the virtues of the virtuous. //18//
Baladeva: In every way, they are enemies of the Veda and of the Lord who is its subject matter; thus he says, "egoism" (ahaṅkāram).

Taking refuge in egoism and the like, they hate and treat with contempt both me—the Lord of all—who resides within the bodies of themselves and others as their controller and sustainer, and the Veda concerning me. They act thus out of disdain.
Envious ones, through crooked arguments, impute faults to the virtues of me and the Veda;
"I alone am independent and act" is pride (*ahaṃkāra*);
"I alone am powerful" is strength (*bala*).
The pride that "there is no one equal to me," the desire that "my will alone accomplishes everything," and the anger that "I myself shall destroy whatever opposes me. //18//
Those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men, who are inauspicious— I hurl them perpetually into demonic wombs alone within the cycles of worldly existence. (19)
Śrīdhara: He says, in two verses beginning with "tān," that there is never any falling away from their demonic nature for them:

"I hurl those hateful and cruel ones perpetually and incessantly into births and deaths upon the paths of worldly existence—specifically into the most cruel demonic wombs such as those of tigers, serpents, and so forth.
The meaning is: "I bestow such a fruit upon those of sinful deeds. (19)
Madhusūdana says "no" to the thought that there might ever be deliverance for them by Your grace; he says "those" (tān):
those who are enemies of the virtuous, being opposed to the path of the righteous, and who are cruel, intent on violence; therefore, they are the lowest of men.

I, the Lord who bestows the fruits of all actions, constantly and perpetually cast down and hurl those who are excessively censurable, who are impure, and who perform impure deeds, into the very realms of cyclic existence along the paths that lead to hell.

It follows that once they have gone to hell, I cast them into the most cruel asuric wombs, such as those of tigers, snakes, and so forth, in accordance with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of their respective actions.
The meaning is that for such traitors, there is no grace from me, the Lord.
And so says the Śruti: "Now, those here whose conduct is vile, they quickly attain a vile womb—either the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7).
"Those of foul conduct," meaning those whose actions are contemptible, "quickly indeed"— as the meaning of the Śruti text states— "attain a foul womb," that is, a contemptible birth.
For this very reason, because [the distribution of results] follows previous and previous karma, there is neither partiality nor cruelty on the part of the Lord.
And thus says the aphorism of the Great Sage: "Inequality and cruelty do not apply, because [the Lord] has regard for [other factors]; for so he shows" (VS 2.1.34).
In this way, the Blessed One causes those very sinful deeds to be performed by them, because the seeds of such deeds exist within them.
