Even though he is compassionate, he does not destroy those deeds, because there is an absence of the accumulation of merit that would destroy them; nor does he cause them to accumulate merit, because they lack the capacity for it.
For the Lord does not produce barley sprouts from stones.
If it is argued that, by virtue of being the Lord, He is able to bring about the fitness of even that which is unfit, [we reply:
He certainly is able, because His resolve is true; provided, however, that He should so resolve.
But He does not will [evil] for those who transgress His commands or who are hostile toward His devotees, because of His own graciousness toward even the wicked.
For this very reason it is heard in scripture: "He indeed makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead upward; and He indeed makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead downward."
He feels affection toward those in whom there is a cause for affection, such as obedience to his commands;

however, he does not feel affection toward those in whom the opposite is the case. Since the effect exists when the cause exists and the effect is absent when the cause is absent, what inconsistency is there in this?

And because of the principle that "it is from another [source], for so it is heard" (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.39), there is no fault, since the Great Illusionist (Mahāmāya) can ultimately bring about some degree of inequality. //19//
Viśvanātha: [Nothing].
Baladeva: He says "those" in two verses to show that for those of demoniac nature, there is no liberation anywhere.

Indeed, I, the Lord of All, who bestows fruits according to their respective actions, perpetually and repeatedly cast them back again and again into demonic wombs of barbarians and hunters, which are characterized by violence, thirst, and the like. (19)
Having entered a demonic womb, these deluded ones, failing to reach Me in birth after birth, O son of Kuntī, go from there to the lowest state. (16.20)

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the demonic" (*āsurīm*), the words "and they, not having attained Me at all" (*te ca mām aprāpyaiva*)—by the use of the particle *eva* (only/at all)—it is shown that even the slightest hope of attaining Me is impossible for them.
It is stated that, failing to reach the true path which is the means for attaining Me, they go from there to even lower births, such as those of worms and insects.
The remainder is clear. //20//
Madhusūdana:
[Objection: "Will not even for them, after many births in succession, there eventually be spiritual welfare? [Reply: No; he says, "The demonic...

Those who have at some time entered a demonic womb are, birth after birth—that is, in every birth—deluded and lacking discrimination due to an abundance of *tamas*; therefore, from that state as well, they go to an even lower destination, the most degraded.
"Without reaching my state"— this implies that there is not even the slightest doubt regarding the attainment of me;
therefore, the meaning is "without reaching the path of the Vedas taught by me."
The particle *eva* indicates the inherent unfitness for attaining the path of the Vedas among animals, stationary beings (*sthāvara*), and so forth.

Thus, the meaning is that, due to an extreme abundance of darkness, having become inherently unfit for attaining the path of the Vedas, they proceed from each preceding inferior birth to an increasingly inferior and lowest birth.
By mentioning his own relationship with the words "O son of Kuntī," He indicates that you have crossed over this [difficulty].
For those who have once entered an asuric womb, there is an acquisition of successively more and more degraded and most degraded wombs,
yet no capacity for remediation, because of the extreme abundance of darkness (*tamas*).

Therefore, as long as the acquisition of a human body remains possible, those seeking the highest good should, with great effort and with all their might, swiftly cultivate divine wealth (*daivī sampad*) while avoiding demonic wealth (*āsuryāḥ sampadaḥ*), which is most grievous; otherwise, upon obtaining the bodies of animals and so forth, one will lack the capacity to practice the means of liberation, and since there will never be a way out, it would be a great calamity.
The collective meaning is "one would fall [into hell]. As it has been said:
"He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that place where there is no medicine, what can he do, being afflicted by pain? (20)
Viśvanātha:
"Without having attained Me" means not by attaining Me [in this life].
At the end of the Dvāpara age, the twenty-eighth cycle of four yugas within the Vaivasvata Manvantara, I have descended as Kṛṣṇa; yet those who take the forms of Kaṃsa and others—

"Even those who, having attained Me, hate Me, shall surely attain liberation. Thus, I, the ocean of boundless compassion, grant even such sinners liberation—which is obtainable through the ripening of devotion and knowledge.

As the scriptures also declare: "That which the sages, with restrained breath, mind, and senses, and firmly joined in yoga, worship in their hearts—even enemies have gone there by mere remembrance" (BhP 10.87.23).
Therefore, my own pre-eminence over all is most excellent, as stated in the *Bhāgavatāmṛta-kārikā*:
"It is indeed clear that as long as My enemies do not attain Me in the form of Kṛṣṇa, for that long they enter the lowest wombs. [LBhāg 1.5.83]
Baladeva: If it be argued that after many births, they might eventually attain liberation from their demoniac womb through your compassion, he says in response: "The demoniac...

Those deluded ones, having entered a demoniac womb in this birth, fail to reach Me and go even further down—from that—to an even more degraded and extremely lowly womb, such as that of a dog and so forth.
By the word "even" (*eva*) in the phrase "failing to reach Me," it is indicated that there is not even the possibility of My compassion [extending to them].
Even a good birth, which is suitable as a means for attaining that [liberation], is difficult to obtain;

and the Śruti declares this thus: "Now, those of evil conduct, by their repeated practice, would indeed fall into an evil womb—either the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7), and so forth.
If it is argued that the Lord, because His volitions are true and so forth, is able to bring about fitness even for one who is unfit, we reply: He certainly would be able to do so if He so willed;

however, He does not will it because of the absence of the seed [of merit]. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras states His lack of partiality [and cruelty] with the words: "There is no partiality or cruelty" (VS 2.1.35), and so on.
Consequently, the two statements beginning with "And therefore, I [saw] them" and so forth are well-established.
These atheists have been shown to be eternally denizens of hell;
however, those Asuras who were cursed, as well as the kṣatriyas who followed them, [beheld] Upendra, Nṛhari, Varāha, and others directly before their eyes.

Even those who, though hostile toward Viṣṇu because He belongs to the side of their own enemies, are devoted to the Vedas and Vedic rites, recognize Him as the Controller of All, the Lord of All, who possesses the power of Time and is imperceptible;
they, having been slain by Upendra and others, gradually abandon their demonic wombs.
And that those slain by Kṛṣṇa are liberated—this the outsiders do not know. //20//
This threefold gate of hell, which is the destroyer of the self— desire, anger, and greed— one should therefore renounce these three. (16.21)
Śrīdhara: Among the demonic defects already mentioned, he says "threefold" to indicate that these three defects, which are the root of all defects, must be avoided by all means.
Desire, anger, and greed—this threefold [set] is the gateway to hell;
for this very reason, it is the destroyer of the self and that which leads to birth in a low womb.
Therefore, one should abandon these three with one's whole being. //21//
Madhusūdana:

Anticipating the objection—"Since the demonic nature (*āsuri-sampad*) possesses infinite varieties, how could it possibly be avoided even within a human lifetime?"—he speaks in brief, saying "threefold" (*trividham*).

This threefold, three-pronged gateway to the attainment of hell is the means [for that end]; it is the root of all demonic nature and the destroyer of the self, bringing about birth in the most inferior wombs by rendering one unfit for any human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
What is that? To this he says: "Desire, anger, and likewise greed. This has been explained previously.
Since these three alone are the root of all misfortune, therefore one should abandon these three.
By the abandonment of these three alone, the entire demonic nature (āsurī saṃpat) becomes abandoned.
It should be understood that the abandonment of these three consists in the obstruction of the activity of that which has arisen through discrimination, and subsequently, its non-arising. //21//
Viśvanātha:
Having thus explained in detail the demonic dispositions as they occur here and there, it was rightly said: "Do not grieve, O Bhārata; you have been born endowed with divine fortune.
Or rather, he asks: is this triad alone natural to the Asuras? To this he says: "Threefold... (21).
Baladeva: Now, if it is asked, "Having heard that the demonic nature is the cause of hell, what should those men who wish to avoid it practice?"—to this he says, "It is threefold.
The meaning is that by avoiding these three, there will be the avoidance of that [demonic nature]. (21)
O son of Kuntī, the man who is freed from these three gates of darkness practices what is beneficial for himself; therefore, he attains the supreme goal. 16.22
Śrīdhara: Regarding renunciation, he states the distinguished result with the words "by these":

a person who is liberated from these three—desire and the rest—which serve as the gates to *tamas* (darkness) and hell, practices such means for his own spiritual welfare as austerity (*tapas*) and yoga;
and through that, he attains liberation. //22//
Madhusūdana says:
To the question, "What would happen to one who abandons these three? he replies with the words beginning with "etair" (by these).
One who is liberated from—meaning separated from—these three, namely desire, anger, and greed, which are gateways to darkness and means for attaining hell.
A person practices for his own welfare— that which is beneficial as revealed by the Vedas— O Kaunteya; for previously, being obstructed by desire and other such impulses,
he does not practice that welfare by which the goal of human life (puruṣārtha) would be accomplished,
and instead practices what is not welfare, by which he would fall away from it.

Now, being free from those obstacles, he does not practice what is unwholesome but practices what is wholesome; thus, having experienced happiness in this world, he attains the supreme goal—liberation—by means of right understanding. //16.22//
Viśvanātha: [Nothing].
Baladeva: He states the result of abandoning those [actions] with the words "by these" (*etair*).
"Welfare" (*śreyaḥ*) refers to the means for attaining welfare, such as the duties of one's own stage of life (*svāśramakarma*).
The supreme goal, which is liberation. //22//
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts under the impulse of desire, attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal. (16.23)
Śrīdhara: He says "he who" because the renunciation of desire and so forth is not possible without the performance of one's own duty (*svadharma*).

Having abandoned the scriptural injunction—the dharma ordained by the Veda—he who acts according to his own whims, as he pleases, does not attain *siddhi*, which is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*);
nor does he attain the supreme goal, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). //23//
Madhusūdana:

Since scripture alone is the cause for both the non-performance of what is not beneficial and the performance of what is beneficial—because these two are to be understood through scripture alone—therefore [the word] "yaḥ" [is used].

Scripture (*śāstra*) is that by which one is taught (*śiṣyate*), instructed (*anuśiṣyate*), or made to understand a previously unknown matter; it consists of the Veda as well as the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth, which depend upon it.

The word "injunction" (*vidhi*) refers to that scriptural injunction— consisting of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth related to that [Brahman]— which has the nature of impelling or restraining, expressed as "one should act" or "one should not act," and which is the cause for the knowledge of what is to be done and what is not to be done; the word "injunction" is used here to indicate that there exists scripture teaching Brahman which is distinct from such injunctions and prohibitions (*niṣedha*).

He who, having cast off [the injunctions] through lack of faith and having abandoned them by acting according to his own whims, does not practice what is prescribed and even practices what is forbidden— he, though performing actions, does not attain perfection, which is the fitness for achieving the goals of human life and the purification of the internal organ.
There is no happiness in this world, nor is there the supreme goal—whether heaven or liberation. //23//
Viśvanātha:
He says "he who" (yaḥ) to show that spiritual welfare belongs only to one who possesses faith, as opposed to one who acts according to his own whims. //23//

Baladeva: The renunciation of desire and so forth cannot occur without one's own duty (*svadharma*), and one's own duty cannot be accomplished without the scripture (*śāstra*). Therefore, the wise person must rely upon the scripture alone; thus he says "he who.
He who acts according to his own whims (*kāmacāra*) does not perform even that which is enjoined.
The meaning is that he performs even what is forbidden.
He does not attain *siddhi*, which is the purification of the heart that serves as the means to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*);
and how could he possibly attain happiness consisting of tranquility, or the supreme goal, which is liberation? //23//
Therefore, let the scripture be your authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
having understood the work prescribed by the ordinances of the scripture, you should perform it here. 24.
Śrīdhara: He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
In this established order—namely, "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done"—your authority (*pramāṇa*) is scripture alone, consisting of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth.

Therefore, having understood the action prescribed by the injunctions of scripture, you ought to perform that action according to your qualification while remaining within this sphere of eligibility for action; for upon that [scripture] is based the purification of the mind, right knowledge, and liberation.
This is the meaning. //24//
In the sixteenth [chapter], it is shown that through the distribution of the prosperity of gods and demons,
the qualification for the knowledge of reality belongs to the one characterized by sattva.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Division between the Divine and Demoniacal Natures," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana: "Because it is thus, therefore...
means that because, through aversion to the scriptures, one's activity is dependent on desire, one becomes unfit for all human goals (puruṣārtha), both of this world and the next.

Therefore, for you who seek your own welfare, regarding the determination of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done—that is, concerning the question of what is duty and what is non-duty—the *śāstra* alone, consisting of the Vedas and the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, etc., which depend upon them, is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the instructor; nothing else, such as your own imagination or the words of the Buddha, is so.
Thus, on this ground of eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*), one should act or refrain from acting according to the injunctions of the *śāstra*, in the form of engagement and desisting.

Having understood the actions prescribed and prohibited as expressed by Vedic terms such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others, you ought to perform the prescribed duties of a Kṣatriya, such as battle and so forth, while avoiding that which is prohibited, until the purification of the mind is attained— this is the meaning. Thus, in this chapter, [the Lord has described] desire, anger, and greed— the great defects which are the root of all demonic qualities, which bring about all misfortune, and which obstruct all well-being.

It has been determined by way of demonstrating the distinction between the two types of prosperity that one who seeks the highest good must, with faith and devotion to the scripture, be intent upon the practice of the teachings therein prescribed.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Distinction Between Divine and Demoniac Prosperity," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp of the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā) composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī. //16//
Viśvanātha: Nothing. Only those who are believers attain the state of the virtuous; they alone are truly good. Atheists go to hell—thus has the meaning of the chapter been explained.
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary which showers the essence of meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, the sixteenth chapter has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous. //16//

Baladeva: Since activity under the sway of desire and the like, by turning one away from the scriptures, causes one to fall from the goals of human life, therefore, regarding the determination of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done—that is, in the matter of what is to be performed and what is not to be performed—the scripture consisting of the Veda alone is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for it is faultless and of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*). It is not, however, a statement imagined by a person who possesses defects such as delusion and the like.

Therefore, by means of words such as the optative (*liṅ*) and the gerundive (*tavya*), which consist of the nature of incitement and prohibition, it is stated: "one should act" or "one should not act" according to the injunctions of the scriptures.

Having understood what action is prescribed and what is forbidden, and having abandoned that which is forbidden, you ought to perform the prescribed actions—such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and battle—in this land of action for the sake of maintaining social order (*loka-saṅgraha*).
Those who are devoted to the meaning of the Vedas attain heaven and eternal liberation.
But those outside the Vedas [go] to the hells; such is the determination of the sixteen.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad.
